q: `makeCounter()` has finished and left the call stack. What happens to its `count`?
options: It stays alive, because the returned function still points at its box
It is thrown away as soon as the call ends
It moves to the global scope
It becomes `undefined`
why: The inner function carries a link to the box where it was made. The link keeps the box alive. That function is a closure.

options: `1 1`: each call makes a new `count` and forgets it
`1 2`: `count` is remembered
`undefined undefined`
why: A local variable dies when its call ends. Each call starts with a new `count` as 0, so both calls give `1`. A closure is what lets a function remember.

why: Every call of `makeCounter` makes a new box. `a` only touches box 1, and `b` only touches box 2. So `a()` gives 1, 2, then 3 later, and `b()` gives 1.

q: The function `read` is made, and then `x` changes. What does `make()()` print?
options: `2`: the function reads `x` from its box each time it runs
`1`: the function copied `x` when it was made
`undefined`
A `ReferenceError`
why: A closure keeps a link to the box, not a copy of the value. When `read` runs, it follows the link and sees the newest `x`.

q: A closure copies the value of a variable at the moment the function is made.
why: No. It keeps a link to the box, so the function always sees the newest value.

options: `"global"`: only where `show` was written matters
`"inside run"`: `run` is the one that calls it
`undefined`
A `ReferenceError`
why: A function reads names from the place where it was written, not from the place that calls it. The interview word is lexical scope.

q: What does this print, after the timers run? Type the three numbers with spaces between them.
why: With `var` there is one box for `i`. The three callbacks all link to it. The loop ends with `i` as 3, and then the callbacks run. With `let`, each pass has its own box, so it would print `0 1 2`.

q: What does a closure give you?
options: Memory between calls, like a counter
Private data that nobody can reach except through your functions
Callbacks that remember the data around them
Faster code, because the variable is copied
why: A closure gives memory, privacy and callbacks that remember. It does not copy anything, and it does not make code faster. A box that stays alive uses memory.

q: Put what happens in the right order.
items: `makeCounter()` is called, and JavaScript makes a new box with `count = 0`
The inner function is made inside that box, so it gets a link to the box
`makeCounter` finishes and leaves the call stack
The box stays alive, because the returned function still points at it
why: A call leaves the stack when it finishes, but its box stays as long as something points at it.

q: In React, this effect runs once because of `[]`. What does the counter show over time?
options: It stays at `1`: the callback keeps the box of render 1, where `count` is 0
It counts `1, 2, 3, ...` every second
It shows `0` forever
React throws an error
why: The timer callback keeps the box of the first render, so it always reads `count = 0` and sets 1 again. That is a stale closure. Fix: `setCount(c => c + 1)`.

q: A timer you never clear can keep a big array alive, even after the function that made it has finished.
why: The timer keeps the callback, the callback keeps the box, and the box keeps the big array. Clear timers and remove listeners when you are done. In React, return a cleanup function from the effect.
